newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary rules seen hindering domestic derivatives.
newsitem.headline: Hungary rules seen hindering domestic derivatives.

text.p: Hungary's relatively restricted capital market may protect the economy from currency troubles but it also hinders the development of domestic derivatives, the Hungarian Forex Club (MFT) said on Thursday.

With profit margins in the main currency markets narrowing, appetite for emerging derivative products was growing, but London-based institututions had seized the initiative as far as the forint was concerned, it said.
"London may become the main market of many forint-denominated derivative products," MFT President Sandor Sebok told a news conference.

MFT official Geza Egyed said interest from foreign investors in forint derivatives had strengthened substantially. Turnover in the market for forint-denominated non-deliverable forward deals (NDFs) -- which appeared in London a few months ago -- had already reached $50 million, he said.
"I think the interest in NDFs will increase," he said. "Many banks (in London) are just now setting up their NDF desks".
Sebok said that turnover on the London market was unlikely to become large enough to influence the Hungarian economy as a whole, but it represented lost business to the Hungarian financial sector.

According to criteria set by the International Monetary Fund, the forint is convertible in all current account deals and for most long-term capital movements. But restrictions on short-term capital movements are still in place.

In the past year, the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) has stabilised domestic markets with cautious policies, tracking the downward trend in market interest rates and inflation small cuts in its own interest rates, Sebok said.

While the NBH will loosen some capital movement rules in 1998, it does not plan to allow foreign investment in short-term instruments such as derivatives and short maturity securities, in order to protect the forint, he said.

Recent currency turbulence in the more liberalised Czech and Polish markets, due in part to the flight of short-term foreign capital, may justify the NBH's cautious stance from a macroeconomic point of view, he said.

However, this conservative attitude may have a negative impact on Hungarian financial institutions, which are unable to benefit from the increased foreign interest in Hungarian derivative products which serve to hedge exchange rate risks, Sebok added.
